Since this alternative does not contain the public works, Citywide housing program and child care center of the proposed plan, an adverse impacts related to these excluded programs will not occur. Therefore, this lack of some of the proposed plan's adverse impacts must be weighed in favor of the alternative. A negative aspect of a pure rehabilitation alternative is that its concentrated attention to physical housing problems fails to reach the whole problem of neighborhood blight. Blighting elements left untouched by this alternative include inadequate park facilities, broken streets and curbs, and the lack of street trees and other physical and social service amenities.
Park Acquisition and Improvement Alternative
This alternative would provide for the park projects included in the CDBG plan, plus those park and recreational proposals made but eliminated by either the Steering Committee or the City Council. Further, the remaining funds would be devoted to park land acquisition and development projects with low and moderate income neighborhoods of San Jose. Use of HUD funds for those alternative objectives is consistent with the applicable provisions of the guidelines which grant assistance for the acquisition of recreational lands and their improvement. The purpose of the Housing and Community Development Act is fulfilled by programs that are directed at providing for the expansion and improvement of community services, and providing for a more rational utilization of land and other resources. The proposed plan achieves the objectives of the act by applying effort chiefly in the housing improvement and public works areas. In contrast, the park alternative would achieve the Act's objectives by focusing attention upon the recreational and aesthetic needs of the population.
A comprehensive park acquisition and improvement plan has the advantage of concentrating recreational efforts into a single program that will meet the community's open space needs in a coordinated rather piecemeal fashion. Concerted park acquisition at this time will avoid higher future land prices or inappropriate private development that would make acquisition at a later date impractical. Park acquisition/developments that do not include the erection of community centers or other large traffic generating structures will show a beneficial net impact on local traffic and air quality levels and will decrease the impact on community services.
Parks that include major community structures and crowd attracting facilities (swimming pools, soccer facilities, large lighted tennis complexes) will have adverse impacts on most environmental categories. In particular, extensive landscaping, revegetation, drainage control, paving, and building disturbance will run the risk of causing negative ecological effects. An increase in on-site facilities can be expected to cause increased demends upon community services and energy use.
